title: Level 3: Abstract Systems (~18–20+ years)
excerpt: At the third level of the abstract tier, the individual becomes capable of constructing abstract systems : integrated coordinations of multiple abstract mappings that specify how several abstractions jointly constrain one another. Where Abstract Mapping involv
html:
At the third level of the abstract tier, the individual becomes capable of constructing abstract systems: integrated coordinations of multiple abstract mappings that specify how several abstractions jointly constrain one another. Where Abstract Mapping involved relating two abstractions (A<->B), Abstract Systems involve understanding how A, B, C, and D all simultaneously interact within a coherent framework. The young adult can now build genuine theories-organized systems of abstract relationships that explain complex phenomena and generate predictions across diverse situations. This is the level at which coherent ideologies, integrated scientific frameworks, systematic philosophies, and unified personal identities become possible. These system are more than the sums of their mappings; they are organized structures in which the mappings themselves are coordinated.

Example 1: Integrated Ethical Framework

At the previous level, the adolescent possesses several moral mappings in relative isolation:

Honesty <-> Kindness (truth-telling can conflict with caring) The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

Loyalty <-> Fairness (favoring friends can conflict with impartiality)

Individual rights <-> Collective welfare (personal freedom can conflict with social good)

Justice <-> Mercy (giving people what they deserve can conflict with compassion)

Each mapping is understood separately; the adolescent can reason about honesty-kindness trade-offs or loyalty-fairness trade-offs, but she has not integrated these into a unified moral framework.

Now, the young adult coordinates these mappings into a systematic ethical theory. She recognizes that moral decisions often involve all of these abstractions simultaneously, and she develops an integrated framework for navigating their complex interactions. This system enables sophisticated moral reasoning:

"In this situation, being honest would be unkind, but being kind would be disloyal to my friend who deserves to know the truth, and fairness suggests that everyone involved has a right to accurate information..."

"My ethical framework prioritizes fairness over loyalty in professional contexts but loyalty over fairness in family contexts-and I can articulate why this is coherent rather than hypocritical"

"When rights and welfare conflict, I tend toward a position that protects basic rights absolutely but allows welfare considerations to adjudicate between non-basic rights"

The young adult can now evaluate moral dilemmas from within an integrated framework, recognize when different parts of her framework generate conflicting prescriptions, and refine the framework to achieve greater coherence. He can also recognize that other people operate from different integrated frameworks and can articulate where his system diverges from theirs.

Example 2: Political Ideology

At the previous level, the adolescent possesses political mappings such as:

Freedom <-> Responsibility

Liberty <-> Equality

Individual <-> Collective

Rights <-> Duties

Security <-> Privacy

These mappings exist somewhat independently: they might reason well about freedom-responsibility without connecting this to their thinking about liberty-equality. Now, the young adult integrates these mappings into a coherent political ideology, a systematic framework that specifies how all of these abstractions relate and that generates consistent positions across diverse political issues. For example, a libertarian-leaning young adult might construct a system in which:

Individual liberty is the foundational value

Rights are primary; duties arise only from voluntary agreements

Equality means equal rights, not equal outcomes

Freedom entails responsibility; those who act irresponsibly bear consequences

Collective action is legitimate only when it protects individual rights

Security concerns cannot override fundamental liberties

A social-democratic young adult might construct a different system:

Equality (including substantive equality of opportunity) is foundational

Rights include positive rights to basic welfare, not just negative rights against interference

Freedom is meaningful only when people have resources to exercise it

Individual flourishing depends on collective provision of public goods

Some liberty can be legitimately constrained to promote equality

Duties to the collective arise from the benefits of social membership

The central achievement of this level is not which ideology is adopted, but that the ideology functions as an integrated system: the various positions cohere, reinforce each other, and derive from shared foundational commitments. The young adult can: The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

Derive positions on novel issues from their framework’s principles

Recognize tensions within their framework and work to resolve them

Articulate why their positions on seemingly unrelated issues (e.g., taxation, free speech, healthcare) actually stem from the same underlying commitments

Engage with alternative ideologies by identifying precisely where the foundational disagreements lie

Example 3: Scientific Systems (Thermodynamics)

At the previous level, the physics student possesses mappings such as:

Energy <-> Work (force applied over distance transfers energy)

Energy <-> Heat (thermal transfer is energy flow)

Temperature <-> Molecular motion (temperature measures average kinetic energy)

Order <-> Entropy (entropy measures disorder)

Each mapping is understood, but they have not been integrated into a unified framework. Now, the student constructs thermodynamics as a system: an integrated theoretical framework in which energy, heat, work, temperature, entropy, and equilibrium all jointly constrain physical processes. The laws of thermodynamics emerge as statements about how these abstractions systematically interrelate: The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure). The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

First Law: Energy is conserved (heat added equals work done plus change in internal energy: ΔU=Q−W\Delta U=Q−W)

Second Law: Entropy of an isolated system never decreases (constrains which energy transformations are possible)

Third Law: Entropy approaches zero as temperature approaches absolute zero (links temperature and entropy at the boundary)

The student can now reason systemically:

"If I want to extract work from a heat engine, I need a temperature differential, but the second law limits my efficiency based on entropy considerations"

"This process conserves energy (first law is satisfied), but it would decrease entropy in an isolated system, so it cannot occur spontaneously"

"The relationships between pressure, volume, temperature, and entropy in this gas can all be derived from the same underlying framework"

The integration is crucial: understanding why a perpetual motion machine is impossible requires coordinating energy conservation (first law), entropy increase (second law), and the relationship between work, heat, and temperature; no single mapping suffices.

Example 4: Psychological System (Personality)

At the previous level, the young adult possesses psychological mappings such as:

Introversion <-> Social anxiety (overlapping behaviors, different causes)

Self-esteem <-> Narcissism (both involve positive self-regard, but differently)

Attachment style <-> Relationship patterns (early bonds shape later relating)

Temperament <-> Character (biological predisposition vs. developed traits)

Now, they integrate these mappings into a systematic theory of personality: a coherent framework for understanding how traits, motivations, developmental history, and situational factors jointly shape human behavior. This integrated understanding enables sophisticated psychological reasoning:

"My social avoidance probably stems from multiple sources: an introverted temperament (biological), an anxious attachment style (developmental), low self-esteem (self-concept), and high rejection sensitivity (motivational). These factors interact; my temperament made me slower to develop social skills, which contributed to anxious attachment, which lowered my self-esteem, which increased my fear of rejection..."

"Understanding someone’s behavior requires considering their traits and their developmental history and the current situation and their goals; no single factor is sufficient"

"Therapy might target different parts of this system: medication could address temperament, attachment work could address relational patterns, cognitive therapy could address self-concept..."

The young adult now has a multi-causal model of personality in which various factors jointly determine outcomes, a significant advance over the previous level’s two-variable thinking.

Example 5: Economic System (Inflation, Rates, Demand, Expectations)

At the previous level, the learner can map single relations like "higher interest rates →\rightarrow lower demand" or "money supply →\rightarrow inflation." Now they coordinate multiple mappings into a macro system with feedback and time lags, commonly integrating: The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

𝐼𝑛𝑡𝑒𝑟𝑒𝑠𝑡 𝑟𝑎𝑡𝑒𝑠→𝑏𝑜𝑟𝑟𝑜𝑤𝑖𝑛𝑔/𝑖𝑛𝑣𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑚𝑒𝑛𝑡→𝑎𝑔𝑔𝑟𝑒𝑔𝑎𝑡𝑒 𝑑𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑\textit{Interest rates} \rightarrow \textit{borrowing/investment} \rightarrow \textit{aggregate demand}

𝐷𝑒𝑚𝑎𝑛𝑑→𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒𝑠 𝑎𝑛𝑑 𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒𝑠\textit{Demand} \rightarrow \textit{prices and wages} (inflation pressure)

𝐸𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠→𝑝𝑟𝑖𝑐𝑒-𝑠𝑒𝑡𝑡𝑖𝑛𝑔/𝑤𝑎𝑔𝑒 𝑏𝑎𝑟𝑔𝑎𝑖𝑛𝑖𝑛𝑔\textit{Expectations} \rightarrow \textit{price-setting/wage bargaining} (self-fulfilling dynamics)

𝑃𝑜𝑙𝑖𝑐𝑦 𝑐𝑟𝑒𝑑𝑖𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦→𝑒𝑥𝑝𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑎𝑡𝑖𝑜𝑛𝑠 𝑠𝑡𝑎𝑏𝑖𝑙𝑖𝑡𝑦\textit{Policy credibility} \rightarrow \textit{expectations stability} (anchoring) The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

This integration generates insights such as:

"A rate hike can reduce inflation even before demand fully cools if it changes expectations"

"Short-run tradeoffs can flip long-run: a stimulus can raise output now but also raise expectations and future inflation"

"The same policy can have different effects depending on whether expectations are anchored"

The learner can now reason more precisely: "If inflation is mostly supply-driven, hiking rates may suppress demand but not fix the bottleneck; you might see lower growth with stubborn inflation unless expectations and wage dynamics also shift."

Example 6: Integrated Identity System

At the previous level, the adolescent can map pairs of abstract self-concepts onto each other: intelligent <-> lazy, confident <-> insecure, independent <-> lonely. But these mappings remain somewhat fragmented; they has multiple "selves" that are partially coordinated but not fully integrated. Now, the young adult constructs an integrated identity: a coherent self-system that organizes multiple abstract self-concepts, roles, values, and goals into a unified sense of "who I am". This integration involves: The relationships in this account are summarized schematically (Figure).

Trait integration: "I am both introverted and ambitious. My introversion shapes how I pursue my ambitions (through individual work rather than networking), and my ambition motivates me to push past my introverted comfort zone when necessary"

Value-role coherence: "My value of authenticity shapes how I enact my roles as student, friend, and employee. I try to be genuine in all contexts, which sometimes creates friction but maintains my integrity"

Temporal integration: "My past experiences of failure, my present commitments, and my future goals form a coherent narrative. I am someone who struggled, learned, and is building toward something meaningful"

Cross-context consistency: "I am recognizably ’the same person’ across different contexts, even though I adapt my behavior. The underlying self-system remains consistent"

Erikson’s concept of "identity achievement" maps onto this accomplishment: the young adult has constructed a systematic self-theory that integrates diverse self-knowledge into a coherent whole. They can explain apparent contradictions in their personality ("I’m both independent and close to my family because..."), articulate how their values guide their choices across domains, and maintain a stable sense of self even as circumstances change.

Example 7: Literary/Historical Interpretation

At the previous level, the literature student might understand mappings such as:

Author’s biography <-> Textual meaning

Historical context <-> Thematic content

Narrative structure <-> Reader response

Symbolism <-> Theme

Now, they construct an integrated system, understanding how authorial intent, historical context, formal structure, symbolic content, reader response, and ideological positioning all jointly shape textual meaning. This enables sophisticated interpretive practice: The concepts are summarized schematically (Figure).

"This novel’s meaning emerges from the intersection of its historical moment (post-war disillusionment), its formal innovations (fragmented narrative), its symbolic patterns (water imagery), and its ideological tensions (class critique undermined by aesthetic elitism); no single lens captures the whole"

"Different interpretive frameworks (formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist) each illuminate certain aspects while obscuring others; a complete reading requires coordinating multiple approaches"

"The author’s intentions matter, but so does the text’s reception history and my own situated reading; meaning is constructed at the intersection of all these factors"

Example 8: Ecological Systems

At the previous level, the environmental science student understands mappings:

Predator <-> Prey populations

Resources <-> Population size

Biodiversity <-> Ecosystem stability

Human activity <-> Environmental change

Now, they construct an integrated system, understanding how energy flow, nutrient cycling, population dynamics, biodiversity, and external perturbations jointly determine ecological outcomes. Systemic reasoning enables:

"Removing this apex predator will increase herbivore populations, which will reduce vegetation, which will increase erosion, which will affect water quality, which will impact aquatic species, which will..."

"Climate change doesn’t just raise temperatures; it shifts precipitation patterns, which affects plant communities, which affects herbivores, which affects predators, while simultaneously changing ocean chemistry, which affects marine food webs..."

"Ecosystem resilience depends on biodiversity, nutrient cycling efficiency, and network structure; interventions must consider all three simultaneously"

The student can now trace cascading effects through interconnected networks and recognize that ecological problems cannot be solved by addressing single variables in isolation.
